abstract: Cytoplasmic incompatibility (CI) is the most widespread reproductive manipulation induced by the endosymbiotic bacteria Wolbachia in arthropods. When infected males mate with uninfected females, some or all embryos die, which favors infected females and drives the spread of the symbiont through host populations. The Wolbachia cif genes that cause CI have been identified, but they do not explain why CI strength varies among host genotypes. The invasive fruit pest Drosophila suzukii illustrates a related paradox: its Wolbachia strain wSuz carries cif genes, yet CI has not been detected in this host species. Combining experimental crosses with genomic and cytological approaches, we show that wSuz does induce CI, with paternal chromosomes showing segregation defects during the first zygotic division. However, CI strength ranges from undetectable to 67% among males from four European host lines. This variation was explained neither by Wolbachia titer in testes nor by the Wolbachia genome, which was nearly identical among isolates and invariant at cif loci. Instead, CI strength depended on the genotype of infected males, whereas the genotype of uninfected females had no detectable effect. Reciprocal F1 and F2 crosses revealed that CI is masked by partially dominant autosomal host suppressors, probably involving a few loci. Masking by host suppressors thus explains the apparent absence of CI in D. suzukii, and host suppressors of CI may also shape the efficacy and evolutionary success of Wolbachia-based pest and vector control strategies.
